title: Domain roadmaps

rule.then: That domain, even at a smaller firm.
Statutory audit with some tax, at the biggest firm that says yes.
Interview for both, one domain per firm at a time.

rule_note: Pick one now and keep one backup. Your real interest shows after a few months of work, and that is normal.
intro: An interviewer checks three things: what your domain is, what an article does there in a normal week, and why this firm's team. Each card answers the first two. The third is your homework: read the firm's service page and one recent piece of its work before you apply.

domains.tagline: How a whole business shows up in its numbers
domains.enjoy: You like seeing how the numbers of a whole business fit together.

first: Small areas first: cash and bank, other income, other expenses, prepaid items.
Draft bank and party confirmations, and track which ones came back.
Vouch invoices against orders, receipt notes and ledgers.
Read last year's working papers to see what was checked, then follow the same approach. Excel is open all day.
later: The big areas: revenue, purchases, inventory, fixed assets, payroll.
Stock counts at the client's warehouse.
Quarterly limited reviews for listed clients.
Draft parts of reports and certificates; sometimes run a small client's file under a senior.
what.note: At many firms the same team also does the tax audit of the same client.

suits: You like seeing how a whole business shows up in its numbers.
Seasons of long days and some travel do not worry you.
You are not yet sure of your domain.
pros: The widest set of exits later.
What you studied in audit and accounts shows up every day.
You see accounting, tax and compliance together.
New industries keep it fresh: listed and unlisted, Ind AS and AS, manufacturing and services.
cons: Documentation is a large part of the job.
Travel to client sites and stock counts.
The first months can feel like admin.

leads.text: Industry finance (reporting, controllership, business finance, FP&A), internal audit, deals (due diligence, valuation), tax with some catch-up, or an audit career.
leads.easier: Listed clients, limited reviews, Excel depth.

domains.season: Peaks after the books close on 31 March: year-end audits, then tax audits. Listed clients add a review every quarter.
questions: Walk me through how a statutory audit runs.
What is materiality? Why is performance materiality set lower?
How would you audit revenue?
Test of controls or test of details? And what is a walkthrough?
A debtor has not replied to your confirmation. What now?

levels.title: Statutory audit 2 · Physical verification of stock
Statutory audit 3 · Fixed assets and depreciation
Statutory audit 6 · Bank, FDs and confirmations
Statutory audit 7 · Materiality, CARO and completion

domains.cv_line: Statutory Audit Work Simulation, MSC Articleship Program | [Month Year]: vouched 20 purchase bills against orders, receipt notes and ledgers and flagged [count] cut-off, approval and GST exceptions.

picks.label: PwC US audit simulation
picks.note: Free, about 3–4 hours, certificate. Purchasing process, walkthrough and RCM tasks.

picks.label: KPMG Canada audit simulation
picks.note: Free, certificate. Excel, controls and substantive testing.

extra: Big firms split audit teams by sector: financial services (banks, NBFCs, insurers, funds) and the rest. Two years in financial services often makes later recruiters see you as an FS person. No preference? A non-FS team usually shows you more kinds of business.

Large networks also run delivery units that support overseas teams. The work there can be checks and documentation with no client contact. Before you apply, read whether the opening is the Indian practice or a delivery unit, and ask what an article in that team did last month.

extra.text: No tool needed: read one listed company's annual report and list its key audit matters and how the auditor responded to each. The Nothing CV shows the line it earns.

domains.tagline: How a business runs from the inside
domains.enjoy: You like understanding how a business runs from inside and talking to the people who run it.

first: Sit in on walkthroughs: one transaction followed end to end with the person who does it.
Write the process narrative.
Fill rows of the risk control matrix: step, what can go wrong, control, owner, frequency, evidence.
Pull samples, test approvals and list the exceptions. Visits to plants and branches.
later: Own a process: purchase, sales, payroll, inventory, fixed assets or treasury.
Draft observations: what we found, what should happen, why it happened, so what, what to do, who and by when.
Help with IFC testing for the auditor's report and, at some firms, SOX testing for US-linked clients.
Help write SOPs.

suits: You want to know how a company really works, from purchase request to payment.
You enjoy talking to the people who run processes.
Travel during normal working hours is fine with you.
pros: You understand a business from inside.
Steadier through the year than statutory audit.
Client interaction early.
A thinking tool every employer values: process, then risk, then control.
cons: Less work on full financial statements.
Fewer finance-side exits than statutory audit.

leads.text: In-house internal audit, risk and controls, controllership, consulting and risk advisory, forensic. Statutory audit after you qualify, with a few months of catch-up.

domains.season: Spread through the year: many assignments are quarterly or continuous. Peaks follow your clients' plans.
questions: Statutory audit or internal audit: what is the difference?
Explain purchase-to-pay in a minute. Name one risk and its control.
What is a risk control matrix?
Design effectiveness or operating effectiveness?
Segregation of duties, maker-checker, compensating control: explain each.

levels.title: Internal audit 1 · Purchase-to-pay walkthrough and control test
Internal audit 2 · RCM and expense claims

domains.cv_line: Internal Audit Work Simulation, MSC Articleship Program | [Month Year]: walked one purchase end to end, tested approval and three-way-match controls on 15 purchases and wrote 2 observations.

picks.label: PwC US audit simulation
picks.note: Free, certificate. Purchasing process, walkthrough and RCM tasks.

picks.label: Deloitte Australia data simulation
picks.note: Free. Data analysis and dashboards for the analytics side.

paid.label: CIA
paid.note: Internal-audit certification. Plan it after real audit work: with a bachelor's degree, certification needs two years of qualifying experience; the exams can come first.

domains.tagline: Apply a provision to a client's facts
domains.enjoy: You enjoy reading a provision and applying it to a client's facts.

first: Computations from the books and return preparation.
Check TDS on a client's payments; monthly deposits, quarterly TDS returns and certificates.
Match the books with the tax-credit statement and the annual information statement before filing.
Schedules for the tax audit, often with the audit team.
later: Notices: intimations, defective-return letters, scrutiny questions, and draft replies.
Research notes when a client asks how a transaction will be taxed.
Submissions and document sets for appeals; sometimes a hearing with a senior. Ask in the interview whether the team does litigation.
what.note: Big firms split direct tax, indirect tax, transfer pricing and M&A tax into separate teams. Mid-size firms usually give you direct and indirect tax both.

suits: You enjoyed tax at Inter.
You like reading a provision and applying it to someone's facts.
You write clearly.
pros: Every business needs it.
Advisory and notice work train your reasoning and drafting.
Mostly office-based.
The new Act rewards people who read the law fresh.
cons: Deadline crunch in return and tax-audit season.
Moving to statutory audit later is harder than the reverse.

leads.text: In-house tax teams, tax advisory, transfer pricing, international tax, a litigation practice.
leads.easier: Advisory and notice work, not only returns.

domains.season: The four advance-tax months (June, September, December, March), quarterly TDS returns, and return and tax-audit season after the audits.
questions: What changed from 1 April 2026, when the Income-tax Act, 2025 started to apply?
What is TDS, and when is it deducted?
TDS on a contractor and on professional fees: which rates?
Why does book profit differ from taxable income?
Advance tax: when, and how much?

levels.title: Direct tax 4 · Computation and advance tax

domains.cv_line: Direct Tax Work Simulation, MSC Articleship Program | [Month Year]: checked [count] tax-audit items (cash payments, TDS, late statutory dues, depreciation) against the books and drafted the notes.

picks.label: PwC US Tax simulation
picks.note: Free, about 3–4 hours, certificate. Book-to-tax differences for a client.

picks.label: Income Tax portal videos
picks.note: Free official videos on return preparation and tax credits.

domains.tagline: Transaction-level rules on a monthly clock
domains.enjoy: You like transaction-level rules and a monthly deadline does not scare you.

first: Collect monthly sales and purchase data and prepare GSTR-1 workings.
Match the purchase register with GSTR-2B and act on supplier invoices in the invoice management system.
Prepare the GSTR-3B summary and list the suppliers to chase.
Check HSN codes, rates, e-invoices and e-way bills.
later: Annual return and reconciliation work.
Refunds for exporters.
Replies to notices: build a bridge from books to returns to source documents.
Advisory questions on rate and classification; customs work at some firms.

suits: You like transaction-level rules and reconciliations.
A monthly deadline does not scare you.
pros: Steady demand in firms and industry.
A young law: many notices and live advisory questions.
You get ownership quickly.
Industry tax teams hire GST people.
cons: Two or three intense days every month around return dates.
A firm that only files returns teaches little. Ask about notices, advisory and customs before you accept.

leads.text: Industry indirect-tax teams, GST advisory and litigation, customs and trade.

domains.season: A few intense days every month around return dates; annual returns once the year's accounts are final.
questions: When do CGST and SGST apply, and when IGST?
Can a business take input tax credit just because it booked the purchase?
Give examples of blocked credit.
Composite supply or mixed supply?
What is reverse charge, and how is it paid?
domains.cv_line: GST Work Simulation, MSC Articleship Program | [Month Year]: prepared GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B workings for a month of [count] invoices and checked input tax credit against GSTR-2B.

picks.label: GSTR-1 tutorial (GST portal)
picks.note: Free official walkthrough of the outward-supply return.

picks.label: GSTR-2B tutorial (GST portal)
picks.note: Free. A mismatch needs a reason before you decide the credit.

domains.tagline: How banks lend, file by file

first: In season, go through advances files: sanction letter, security documents, latest stock statement.
Work out drawing power; check how many days each account is overdue and whether it is classified right.
Check interest and charges were applied; verify cash and securities at the branch.
Review suspense and sundry accounts and fill the long-form report checklists.
later: Concurrent audit, at firms that do it: month-by-month checks of a branch, such as whether processing fees and penal charges were charged as sanctioned.
what.note: Most firms do this inside an audit team. A separate bank-audit department is less common.

suits: Banking and credit interest you.
A short, intense season with travel is fine.
pros: Concentrated learning on how banks lend.
Carries into NBFC and bank roles.
Concurrent audit adds year-round work at some firms.
cons: Rarely a full domain on its own.

leads.text: Bank and NBFC credit and risk roles, financial-services audit, concurrent and internal audit in banks.

domains.season: Short and intense: year-end branch audits right after 31 March. Concurrent audits run every month.
questions: When does a loan become a non-performing asset?
Sanction, drawing power and outstanding: is this cash-credit account within its limit?
Name the asset classes for advances.
Statutory branch audit or concurrent audit: what is the difference?
A branch keeps missing small processing fees. How would you look at it?

levels.title: Bank audit 1 · Drawing power and classification

domains.enjoy: You like tax plus numbers plus cross-border business.

first: Collect the client's related-party transactions.
Join interviews on functions, assets and risks, and write them up.
Run or check comparable searches; seniors usually decide.
later: Compute margins and the arm's-length range.
Prepare documentation and the data for the accountant's report.
Help with assessments in some teams.
what.note: Mostly a big-firm team, busy all year.

suits: Tax, numbers and cross-border business all interest you.
You are patient with documentation.
pros: A specialist skill.
The arm's-length idea works the same way in many countries, so the skill travels.
Dedicated teams at large firms.
cons: Narrower exits outside TP and international tax.

leads.text: TP and international tax at firms, group tax in multinationals.

questions: What is transfer pricing, and why does the law care?
What is an associated enterprise?
Which methods set the arm's-length price?
Why is TNMM used so often?

domains.tagline: The tax side of mergers and deals
domains.enjoy: You genuinely like tax law and research.

first: Research the tax side of transactions: mergers, demergers, slump sales, buybacks, capital reductions.
Tax due diligence on a target: returns filed, notices under control, losses carried forward with support.
Read share purchase agreements for the tax clauses.
later: Build a financial snapshot of a company from its balance sheet and P&L, and brainstorm options.
Make the slide deck a senior, then a manager, then a partner reviews before it reaches the client.
what.note: Office-based, little travel. Pressure comes near a deal's closing date and after the Budget.

suits: You genuinely like tax law.
You enjoy reading a section, then case law, then a commentary to decide a client's case.
pros: No two assignments repeat.
Deep income-tax learning that helps CA Final direct tax.
Close work with seniors; strong writing and slide skills.
Predictable office hours most of the year.
cons: Very few seats, often filled through people who already work there.
Exits mostly within tax and deal advisory.
Less useful if you plan a general practice later.

leads.text: M&A tax and deal advisory, structuring roles. Fewer industry routes, because industry has little M&A tax work.

questions: What is a capital asset? Is stock-in-trade one? What if stock is converted into a capital asset?
What is a slump sale, and how is the gain worked out, broadly?
How is a buyback taxed now, and how did that change?
Which transfers are not treated as transfers for capital gains, for example in a merger?
Buyback or capital reduction under company law: limits and approvals?

picks.note: Free, certificate. Book-to-tax thinking.

domains.enjoy: FM and SFM were your favourite, and Excel models excite you.

first: Pull a few months of daily share prices to work out a stock's beta.
Gather comparable listed companies and their multiples.
Look up cost-of-capital inputs on the firm's databases.

later: Build parts of DCF models, then whole models.
Draft report sections and present workings to seniors.

suits: FM and SFM were your favourite.
Logic and Excel models excite you.
You like seeing many different businesses.
pros: Varied work across industries.
A strong modelling skill.
A natural base for deals, due diligence, corporate development and, with effort, IB.

Little tax exposure, and industry roles often want some.

Two ways to get a terminal value?

Analyse customer concentration and receivable ageing.
Draft findings that a senior turns into the report.

domains.tagline: Follow the money, find what is wrong
domains.enjoy: You can picture how someone would cheat a process and where the money would go.

first: Run data checks on ledgers and payment files: duplicates, round sums, entries on holidays.

later: Help with background checks on vendors and other parties.

domains.tagline: Structure messy problems, explain them simply
domains.enjoy: You like structuring messy problems and explaining them simply.

first: At most firms, "risk advisory" is the internal audit, IFC and SOX work on the Internal audit card.
Where a consulting seat exists: research on markets and competitors, and data analysis.
later: Process mapping and KPI dashboards.
Slide decks and notes for client meetings.

suits: You think in structures.
You can explain a messy problem simply.
pros: Problem-solving across many kinds of business.
Data, slides and structured thinking: skills every employer wants.
cons: Top strategy firms mostly hire after qualification, alongside MBAs.
The usual articleship routes into consulting are internal audit and risk advisory, tax advisory or statutory audit.

questions.q: How would you break down "profit fell this year"?
questions.a: Draw an issue tree. Profit = revenue − costs; revenue = price × volume; costs = fixed + variable. Go down each branch with data, and keep the branches separate and, together, complete.

questions.q: Name a framework for an industry and use it.
questions.a: Porter's five forces: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power. Apply them to one industry you know, one line each.

questions.q: SWOT or PESTLE: what is the difference?
questions.a: SWOT looks at one business, inside and out. PESTLE scans the world outside it: political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental.
A small share of causes often drives most of a result. Find those few and fix them first.

questions.q: Guesstimate: how many cars are serviced in your city each month?
questions.a: Say the structure before any number: people in the city, then households with a car, then services a car needs in a year, divided by 12. State each assumption aloud, round sensibly, and check the answer feels right.

domains.cv_line: Consulting Work Simulation, MSC Articleship Program | [Month Year]: broke a profit fall into price, volume and cost drivers and made one recommendation.

extra.text: Few article seats here? Industrial training later in your articleship is the second door, under ICAI's conditions. A finance role in industry also builds what consulting needs.

questions.a: Forecast revenue, costs, capex and working capital; work out free cash flow; discount it at WACC; add a discounted terminal value; then bridge to equity value.

questions.q: Equity value or enterprise value: what is the difference?
questions.a: Enterprise value is what the whole business is worth to everyone who funds it: equity value plus debt, preference capital and minority interest, minus cash.

questions.q: Which multiple would you use for a loss-making start-up?
questions.a: Revenue or user-based multiples, recent funding rounds and a few scenario DCFs. Cross-check the methods against each other.
A draft offer document is filed with SEBI; after its observations comes the final offer document with a price band, then book-building, allotment and listing. Merchant bankers run it.

questions.q: Why can a company with positive EBITDA still go bust?
questions.a: EBITDA ignores capex, interest, debt repayments and one-off cash outflows. When those are bigger than the cash the business makes, it runs out of money.

rows.text: Raising money and advising on deals.

rows.label: Managed services or business outsourcing
rows.text: Outsourced process work for clients. Ask what articles do before you pick it.

lockin: Your articleship does not lock you in. People move from M&A tax to business finance, from statutory audit to business finance, from a mid-size tax practice to an industry GST team. What you learn and can explain matters more than the label.

glossary.meaning: The programme's firm shortlist. Big 4: Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG. Big 6 adds BDO India and Grant Thornton Bharat. Big 10 adds RSM India, Lodha & Co., S S Kothari Mehta & Co. and Sahni Natarajan & Bahl.
Financial services clients (banks, NBFCs, insurers, funds) and everyone else.
Record to report: from entries to financial statements.
Procure to pay: from purchase request to payment.
Order to cash: from customer order to money received.
Hire to retire: the payroll and people process.
In internal audit, the risk control matrix. In GST, the same letters mean reverse charge.
Internal financial controls; internal controls over financial reporting.
A US controls law that some India-based companies of US-listed groups test for.
Test of controls (did the control run?) and test of details (is the amount right?).
Following one transaction end to end to understand a process and its controls.
Prepared by client: the documents the client is asked to provide.
Agreeing a number to its source and marking it as checked.
Carrying a balance or headcount from one date to another through the movements.
A senior's approval that a piece of work is complete and reviewed.
The auditor's quarterly review of a listed company's results: less than an audit.
Long form audit report: the detailed checklist report in a bank branch audit.
Memorandum of changes: the auditor's list of changes to a bank branch's accounts.
Financial accounting advisory services: accounting advisory, often Ind AS and IPO readiness.
Virtual CFO: a part-time finance head for smaller clients.
Financial and tax due diligence on a target before a deal.
Quality of earnings: how much of reported profit will repeat.
The normal level of working capital agreed in a deal; the price moves if closing working capital differs.
Virtual data room; information request list, the list of documents asked for in a deal.
Working for the buyer or for the seller in a deal.
Transfer pricing; arm's-length price; associated enterprise.
The tax side of a deal, versus the deal itself.
Discounted cash flow; weighted average cost of capital; enterprise value.
Equity research: analysing listed companies for investors.
Outsourced process work a firm runs for its clients.
A unit of a large network that supports its overseas teams from India.
